# Tao (Jonas) Chen

> Tao (Jonas) Chen is Provost's Chair Professor in Finance at Nanyang Business School, NTU Singapore. His research covers sustainable finance; FinTech, AI, and finance; and how investors and monitors shape corporate policy.

Provost's Chair Professor in Finance, Nanyang Business School, Nanyang Technological University (NTU), Singapore. Email: jtchen@ntu.edu.sg.

## Publications — Sustainable Finance

How environmental, social and governance forces shape firm behaviour: pollution and environmental policy, social responsibility, tax practices, and the oversight of managers.

### Ecological integrity of avoided deforestation projects

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/ecological-integrity-avoided-deforestation-ncc-2026/
- Authors: Kelly Ong, Tao Chen, Zhimin Chen, Carlos T. Pérez-Brito, Yiwen Zeng
- Published: Nature Climate Change 16(7): 769–773, 2026. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1038/s41558-026-02657-2
- PDF: not yet publicly available
- Keywords: avoided deforestation; carbon credits; ecological integrity; biodiversity; nature-based climate solutions; voluntary carbon market
- In one sentence: Most accredited avoided-deforestation carbon projects do not maintain the ecological condition of forests better than comparable unprotected areas.
- Summary: Avoided-deforestation projects generate carbon credits by reducing forest loss, but it is unclear whether they also keep forests ecologically healthy. The paper compiles 196 accredited projects from major voluntary carbon registries and compares project areas with matched control areas in the same biome, excluding a 10-km zone around each project to allow for local leakage. For the 133 projects with good matches, it evaluates five indicators of ecological integrity: biodiversity intactness, forest landscape integrity, fragmentation, canopy height and net greenhouse-gas flux. Most projects show mixed, negligible or negative effects relative to controls, which points to shortcomings that limit these projects’ ability to safeguard ecosystems and sequester carbon.

### Minimum Wages, State Ownership, and Corporate Environmental Policies

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/minimum-wages-state-ownership-jfqa-2025/
- Authors: Tao Chen, Xi Xiong, Kunru Zou
- Published: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 60(6): 2921–2951, 2025. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022109024000644
- PDF: https://taochen.org/papers/chen-xiong-zou-2025-jfqa.pdf (Published version (open access))
- Keywords: minimum wages; state ownership; corporate environmental policy; pollution; China; labor market policy
- In one sentence: Minimum wage increases lead industrial firms to pollute more and to cut abatement, and state ownership reduces these effects.
- Summary: The paper studies how labour-market policy affects corporate environmental behaviour, using minimum wage discontinuities at county borders in China. Minimum wage increases lead industrial firms to pollute more and reduce abatement efforts. State ownership mitigates these effects, consistent with state owners internalising the externality, and the effects are weaker after provinces raise pollution discharge fees. The effects are stronger for firms more sensitive to minimum wages, with less market power or tighter financial constraints, and for subsidiaries of non-listed companies. The results show an unintended environmental consequence of labour-market policy.

### Labor unionization and real earnings management: Evidence from labor elections

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/labor-unionization-real-earnings-plos-one-2024/
- Authors: Vivek Astvansh, Beibei Wang, Tao Chen, Jimmy Chengyuan Qu
- Published: PLOS ONE 19(2): e0292889, 2024. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0292889
- PDF: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/file?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0292889&type=printable (Published version (open access))
- Keywords: labor unions; unionization elections; real earnings management; regression discontinuity
- In one sentence: Firms whose workers narrowly vote to unionize reduce real earnings management compared with firms where the vote narrowly fails.
- Summary: The paper studies how labour unionization affects real earnings management, exploiting close-call union elections. In a local regression discontinuity analysis, firms where the union narrowly passes the 50% threshold significantly reduce real earnings management relative to firms where it narrowly fails, consistent with greater labour power putting pressure on managers. The effect is stronger for firms headquartered in right-to-work states and when managers face less pressure to manage earnings. A global parametric regression discontinuity analysis and tests using industry-level unionization support the external validity of the results.

### The social cost of investor distraction: Evidence from institutional cross-blockholding

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/social-cost-investor-distraction-plos-one-2023/
- Authors: Vivek Astvansh, Tao Chen, Jimmy Chengyuan Qu
- Published: PLOS ONE 18(12): e0286336, 2023. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0286336
- PDF: https://journals.plos.org/plosone/article/file?id=10.1371/journal.pone.0286336&type=printable (Published version (open access))
- Keywords: institutional cross-blockholding; investor distraction; corporate social responsibility; institutional investors
- In one sentence: When institutional investors hold blocks in several firms in an industry, they are distracted, and the social performance of those firms suffers.
- Summary: Institutional investors often hold blocks of shares in several firms in the same industry. The paper asks whether such cross-blockholding distracts investors from firms’ non-financial activities, using corporate social responsibility as the setting. Cross-held firms perform worse on social responsibility than other firms, and a quasi-natural experiment based on mergers between institutional blockholders supports a causal interpretation. Using EDGAR search volume and shareholder proposals on socially responsible investment as proxies, the paper shows that the effect comes mainly from investor distraction when investors hold several blocks at once.

### Bank deregulation and corporate environmental performance

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/bank-deregulation-corporate-environmental-wd-2023/
- Authors: Shiyi Chen, Tao Chen, Pingyi Lou, Hong Song, Chenyu Wu
- Published: World Development 161: 106106, 2023. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.worlddev.2022.106106
- PDF: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm?abstractid=3633696 (Working-paper version (SSRN), titled “Bank Competition and Corporate Environmental Performance”)
- Keywords: bank deregulation; bank branching; corporate environmental performance; pollution; China
- In one sentence: After bank branching deregulation in China, firms more exposed to the deregulation emit less pollution per unit of output.
- Summary: The paper examines how bank deregulation affects corporate environmental performance, using bank branching deregulation in China and firm-level data on toxic emissions. Firms more exposed to the deregulation lower their chemical oxygen demand (COD) emission intensity compared with less exposed firms. Treated firms also become more productive and reduce the share of tangible assets in total assets, which points to technology upgrading and a change in asset mix as the channels. The paper documents an environmental consequence of banking liberalisation that is relevant for developing countries reforming their banking sectors.

### The Unintended Consequence of Land Finance: Evidence from Corporate Tax Avoidance

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/unintended-consequence-land-finance-ms-2022/
- Authors: Tao Chen, Youchao Tan, Jinghua Wang, Cheng (Colin) Zeng
- Published: Management Science 68(11): 8319–8342, 2022. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2021.4191
- PDF: https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/pdf/10.1287/mnsc.2021.4191 (Published version (open access))
- Keywords: land finance; tax avoidance; tax enforcement; local government; China
- In one sentence: When Chinese local governments lose land-sale revenue, they enforce taxes more strictly and local firms avoid less tax.
- Summary: Using a large sample of unlisted industrial firms in China, the paper shows that a decrease in local governments’ land transfer revenues leads to lower tax avoidance by firms in their jurisdiction. The effect is stronger in cities that depend more on land finance, where government intervention is greater, and where political leaders have stronger promotion incentives, and it is weaker for politically connected firms. The mechanism is intensified tax enforcement following the loss of land revenue. The paper identifies land finance as a previously underexplored determinant of corporate tax avoidance.

### Globalization and U.S. Corporate Tax Policies: Evidence from Import Competition

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/globalization-us-corporate-tax-ms-2022/
- Authors: Tao Chen, Chen Lin, Xiang Shao
- Published: Management Science 68(8): 6145–6162, 2022. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2021.4121
- PDF: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm?abstractid=3135205 (Working-paper version (SSRN))
- Keywords: globalization; import competition; tax avoidance; Permanent Normal Trade Relations; U.S. manufacturing
- In one sentence: U.S. manufacturers facing more competition from Chinese imports increase their tax-reduction activities.
- Summary: The paper studies how globalisation affects the tax policies of U.S. manufacturing firms, using the U.S. grant of Permanent Normal Trade Relations to China as a quasi-natural experiment. Firms with greater exposure to Chinese imports significantly increase tax-reduction activities, especially firms with more managerial slack, less diversified product markets and faster-changing industries. Exposed firms are also more likely to acquire subsidiaries in low-tax regions and to show signs of transfer pricing. Tax-reduction activity falls after the 2017 U.S. tax cut and after tariffs on Chinese imports rise.

### Does credit rating conservatism matter for corporate tax avoidance?

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/credit-rating-conservatism-matter-af-2021/
- Authors: Tao Chen, Sidney Leung, Lingmin Xie
- Published: Accounting & Finance 61(4): 5681–5730, 2021. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1111/acfi.12773
- PDF: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm?abstractid=2966014 (Working-paper version (SSRN))
- Keywords: credit rating conservatism; tax avoidance; Dodd-Frank Act; sovereign downgrade; quasi-natural experiment
- In one sentence: When credit rating agencies become more conservative, firms engage in more tax planning.
- Summary: The paper studies whether credit rating conservatism affects corporate tax avoidance, using the passage of the Dodd–Frank Act and the US sovereign downgrade as quasi-natural experiments. In both settings, treated firms engage in more tax-planning activities than control firms. In the larger Dodd–Frank sample, the effects are concentrated among firms with more existing tax-planning capacity, less use of external financing, greater reliance on rating information and weaker external monitoring. The evidence indicates that rating conservatism plays a role in firms’ tax-avoidance decisions.

### Institutional shareholders and corporate social responsibility

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/institutional-shareholders-corporate-social-jfe-2020/
- Authors: Tao Chen, Hui Dong, Chen Lin
- Published: Journal of Financial Economics 135(2): 483–504, 2020. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2019.06.007
- PDF: https://dr.ntu.edu.sg/server/api/core/bitstreams/233ea276-ae9e-48aa-a0e6-3da3f18295f3/content (Accepted manuscript (DR-NTU repository))
- Keywords: institutional ownership; corporate social responsibility; Russell index reconstitution; shareholder attention; ESG
- In one sentence: Institutional shareholders improve the social and environmental performance of the firms they own.
- Summary: The paper uses two quasi-natural experiments to identify the effect of institutional shareholders on corporate social responsibility (CSR). An exogenous increase in institutional ownership from Russell index reconstitutions improves portfolio firms’ CSR performance, and firms receive lower CSR ratings when their shareholders are exogenously distracted. The effect is stronger in CSR categories that are financially material. Institutional shareholders influence CSR through CSR-related shareholder proposals. The results suggest that institutional investors can generate real social impact.

### Does Information Asymmetry Affect Corporate Tax Aggressiveness?

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/information-asymmetry-affect-corporate-jfqa-2017/
- Authors: Tao Chen, Chen Lin
- Published: Journal of Financial and Quantitative Analysis 52(5): 2053–2081, 2017. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022109017000576
- PDF: https://dr.ntu.edu.sg/server/api/core/bitstreams/62dbf0a8-be0d-4091-b4f0-bfcd5bfcdaea/content (Published version (DR-NTU repository))
- Keywords: information asymmetry; tax avoidance; tax aggressiveness; analyst coverage; broker closures and mergers
- In one sentence: Firms avoid taxes more aggressively after they lose analyst coverage, which raises information asymmetry.
- Summary: The paper asks whether information asymmetry affects corporate tax avoidance. It uses reductions in analyst coverage caused by broker closures and mergers, with a difference-in-differences matching estimator. Firms avoid tax more aggressively after losing an analyst. The effect is driven by firms with greater existing tax-planning capacity (such as a tax-haven presence), smaller initial coverage and fewer peer firms. It is stronger in industries where reputation matters more and in firms that face less monitoring from tax authorities.

### Institutions, board structure, and corporate performance: Evidence from Chinese firms

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/institutions-board-structure-corporate-jcf-2015/
- Authors: Tao Chen
- Published: Journal of Corporate Finance 32: 217–237, 2015. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcorpfin.2014.10.009
- PDF: https://dr.ntu.edu.sg/server/api/core/bitstreams/b4b3ac62-908e-4345-b740-a34203a173dd/content (Accepted manuscript (DR-NTU repository))
- Keywords: board structure; outside directors; property rights; institutions; firm performance; China
- In one sentence: In China, weaker property-rights protection is associated with more outsiders on corporate boards, and in that environment outsiders improve firm performance.
- Summary: The paper studies how the institutional environment, such as property-rights protection, shapes the size and composition of corporate boards in China, and how board structure in turn affects performance. Using a World Bank survey of 2,400 public and private firms in 18 Chinese cities, it finds that a weaker “helping hand” from government is associated with more outside directors, both in number and as a share of the board. This holds after controlling for firm complexity, growth opportunities, CEO characteristics, ownership and potential endogeneity. When firms operate in a weak property-rights environment, more outsiders on the board improve corporate performance.

### Do analysts matter for governance? Evidence from natural experiments

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/analysts-matter-governance-natural-jfe-2015/
- Authors: Tao Chen, Jarrad Harford, Chen Lin
- Published: Journal of Financial Economics 115(2): 383–410, 2015. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jfineco.2014.10.002
- PDF: https://dr.ntu.edu.sg/server/api/core/bitstreams/6299832e-1610-46a8-8bd0-dcaa27a56f6e/content (Accepted manuscript (DR-NTU repository))
- Keywords: financial analysts; corporate governance; monitoring; executive compensation; earnings management; acquisitions
- In one sentence: Financial analysts act as monitors: when a firm loses analyst coverage, its managers behave in ways that are worse for outside shareholders.
- Summary: Using broker closures and mergers as exogenous shocks to analyst coverage, the paper estimates the causal effect of analysts on managerial expropriation of outside shareholders. After a firm loses coverage, shareholders value its cash holdings less, its CEO receives higher excess compensation, management is more likely to make value-destroying acquisitions, and managers engage more in earnings management. The effects are driven mainly by firms with smaller initial coverage and less product-market competition, and CEO pay becomes less sensitive to performance. The findings support the view that analysts play an important governance role.


## Publications — FinTech, AI, and Finance

How financial technology and artificial intelligence change access to credit, innovation, and the way consumers respond to technology-driven markets.

### Cultural Lag, Consumer Literacy, and Coping in AI-Enabled Advertising: A Theoretical Explication and Managerial Solutions

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/cultural-lag-consumer-literacy-ja-2026/
- Authors: Chen Lou, Xuan Zhou, Elison Ai Ching Lim, Tao Chen, Edson C. Tandoc, Diotima Chattoraj
- Published: Journal of Advertising 55(4): 439–461, 2026. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1080/00913367.2026.2652377
- PDF: https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/pdf/10.1080/00913367.2026.2652377 (Published version (open access))
- Keywords: AI-enabled advertising; artificial intelligence; cultural lag; persuasion knowledge model; consumer literacy
- In one sentence: Consumers’ beliefs, literacy, public policy and public education lag behind AI-enabled advertising, and most people cannot tell AI-enabled ads from traditional ones without disclosure.
- Summary: Guided by cultural lag theory and the persuasion knowledge model, the paper studies how consumers understand and cope with AI-enabled advertising in ad creation and ad placement. It draws on 12 focus groups across four generational cohorts (Gen Z, Millennials, Gen X and Baby Boomers). It identifies four cultural aspects that lag behind AI-enabled advertising: consumer beliefs, consumer knowledge and literacy, public policy, and public education. Most participants cannot distinguish AI-enabled ads from traditional ads without disclosure, and they use a range of coping strategies to deal with concerns about AI-created ads and data-privacy risks in AI-driven ad placement.

### What influences demand for Buy Now, Pay Later credit?

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/influences-demand-buy-now-el-2024/
- Authors: Tao Chen, Ben R. Marshall, Nhut H. Nguyen, Nuttawat Visaltanachoti
- Published: Economics Letters 242: 111857, 2024. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.econlet.2024.111857
- PDF: https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0165176524003410/pdfft (Published version (open access))
- Keywords: Buy Now, Pay Later; consumer credit; interest rates; responsible lending; New Zealand
- In one sentence: In New Zealand, demand for Buy Now, Pay Later credit is higher among single, younger and lower-income people and falls when interest rates rise.
- Summary: The paper studies the determinants of demand for Buy Now, Pay Later (BNPL) credit using a comprehensive New Zealand database, measuring demand both in absolute terms and relative to total personal lending demand. BNPL is more popular with single people, younger people and those on lower incomes. Both absolute and relative BNPL demand are negatively related to interest rates. Demand fell around changes to responsible-lending legislation, even though those changes were not specific to BNPL, and rose after COVID-19 lockdowns ended.

### Authentically Fake? How Consumers Respond to the Influence of Virtual Influencers

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/authentically-fake-consumers-respond-ja-2023/
- Authors: Chen Lou, Siu Ting Josie Kiew, Tao Chen, Tze Yen Michelle Lee, Jia En Celine Ong, ZhaoXi Phua
- Published: Journal of Advertising 52(4): 540–557, 2023. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1080/00913367.2022.2149641
- PDF: not yet publicly available
- Keywords: virtual influencers; influencer advertising; uncanny valley; uses and gratifications; artificial intelligence
- In one sentence: Followers see virtual influencers as uncanny but “authentically fake”: effective for brand awareness, but weak at persuading people to buy.
- Summary: Guided by the uses-and-gratifications approach and uncanny valley theory, the paper studies why people follow virtual influencers (computer-generated social media characters) and how they respond to them. It identifies six motivations for following: novelty, information, entertainment, surveillance, aesthetics, and integration and social interaction. Most followers perceive virtual influencers as uncanny and “authentically fake”, but accept their staged fabrication, and curated flaws and self-justification soften the uncanny-valley effect. Virtual influencers are seen as effective for building brand image and awareness but lack the persuasive power to drive purchase intention, because of low authenticity, low similarity to followers and weak parasocial relationships.

### Finance and Firm Volatility: Evidence from Small Business Lending in China

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/finance-firm-volatility-small-ms-2022/
- Authors: Tao Chen, Yi Huang, Chen Lin, Zixia Sheng
- Published: Management Science 68(3): 2226–2249, 2022. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1287/mnsc.2020.3942
- PDF: https://taochen.org/papers/chen-huang-lin-sheng-2022-ms.pdf (Accepted manuscript, October 2020)
- Keywords: FinTech credit; small business lending; firm volatility; Alibaba; regression discontinuity; China
- In one sentence: Access to FinTech credit on Alibaba’s platform makes small online businesses’ sales less volatile and makes them less likely to exit.
- Summary: Alibaba’s online trading platform provides FinTech credit to millions of micro, small and medium-sized enterprises. Using daily sales data and an internal credit-score threshold that governs who receives credit, the paper applies a fuzzy regression discontinuity design to estimate the causal effect of credit access on firm volatility. Credit access significantly reduces sales volatility, especially for firms with fewer alternative sources of financing, and firms with FinTech credit are less likely to go bankrupt or exit later. Firms with credit invest more in advertising and in product and sector diversification, particularly during downturns, which are the channels through which credit reduces volatility.

### Impact of Competition on Innovations of IT Industry: An Empirical Investigation

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/impact-competition-innovations-it-jmis-2021/
- Authors: Tao Chen, Hsing Kenneth Cheng, Yong (Jimmy) Jin, Shengli Li, Liangfei Qiu
- Published: Journal of Management Information Systems 38(3): 647–666, 2021. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1080/07421222.2021.1962590
- PDF: not yet publicly available
- Keywords: product market competition; innovation; patents; IT industry; import tariffs
- In one sentence: More product-market competition leads IT firms to produce more, and more highly cited, patents.
- Summary: The paper examines the causal relationship between product-market competition and innovation in the information technology (IT) industry, measuring innovation by patent counts (quantity) and non-self citations (quality). Using the Herfindahl–Hirschman Index and natural experiments, it finds robust evidence that competition increases innovation. After import tariff cuts raised competition, patents per IT firm rose by 27.3 percent and non-self citations per firm by 38.2 percent on average, with larger effects in more competitive sectors. The authors attribute the positive effect mainly to a parallel-search effect and note that lower import barriers may bring welfare gains through innovation.

### Financial innovation: The bright and the dark sides

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/financial-innovation-bright-dark-jbf-2016/
- Authors: Thorsten Beck, Tao Chen, Chen Lin, Frank M. Song
- Published: Journal of Banking & Finance 72: 28–51, 2016. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbankfin.2016.06.012
- PDF: https://dr.ntu.edu.sg/server/api/core/bitstreams/5f4863e8-4fb2-4125-be36-91751b45f372/content (Accepted manuscript (DR-NTU repository))
- Keywords: financial innovation; bank fragility; bank growth; economic growth; financial crisis
- In one sentence: Financial innovation is associated with faster bank growth but also with greater bank fragility, and on net with higher economic growth where growth opportunities are better.
- Summary: Using data from 32 countries over 1996–2010, the paper assesses how financial innovation relates to bank growth and fragility and to economic growth. Several measures of financial innovation, both broad and specific, are associated with faster bank growth but also with higher bank fragility and worse bank performance during the recent crisis. These effects are stronger in countries with larger securities markets and more restrictive regulation. Despite these mixed findings, the net effect on economic growth appears positive: financial innovation is associated with higher growth in countries and industries with better growth opportunities.


## Publications — Investors, Monitors and Corporate Policy

How analysts, owners, regulators and governments shape corporate investment, risk-taking and firm value.

### Analyst coverage, executive compensation and corporate risk‐taking: Evidence from property–casualty insurance firms

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/analyst-coverage-executive-compensation-jri-2023/
- Authors: Tao Chen, Shinichi Kamiya, Pingyi Lou, Andreas Milidonis
- Published: Journal of Risk and Insurance 90(4): 899–939, 2023. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1111/jori.12437
- PDF: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm?abstractid=3778633 (Working-paper version (SSRN), titled “Analyst Coverage and Corporate Risk-Taking”)
- Keywords: analyst coverage; risk-taking; executive compensation; property-casualty insurance; monitoring
- In one sentence: When property–casualty insurers lose analyst coverage, they take more risk, especially where managers’ pay rewards risk-taking.
- Summary: Using exogenous drops in analyst coverage caused by broker closures and mergers, the paper tests the causal effect of analyst coverage on risk-taking in an opaque industry, property–casualty insurance. After losing coverage, insurers’ risk increases on several book-based and market-based measures, including tail and default risk. The results are driven by firms whose managers have stronger risk-taking incentives in their compensation, and they are stronger for more opaque firms and firms with weaker policyholder monitoring. Risk rises through at least one risk-taking action, such as investing in higher-risk bonds.

### Dual Ownership and Risk-Taking Incentives in Managerial Compensation

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/dual-ownership-risk-taking-rof-2023/
- Authors: Tao Chen, Li Zhang, Qifei Zhu
- Published: Review of Finance 27(5): 1823–1857, 2023. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1093/rof/rfad007
- PDF: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm?abstractid=3427030 (Working-paper version (SSRN))
- Keywords: dual ownership; executive compensation; risk-taking incentives; inside debt; institutional investors
- In one sentence: When more of a firm is owned by institutions that hold both its shares and its bonds, CEO pay is designed to encourage less risk-taking.
- Summary: The paper studies how interactions among shareholders, creditors and managers shape executive compensation. Firms with more ownership by “dual holders”, institutional investors that hold both the firm’s equity and its bonds, use less risk-inducing compensation, with fewer stock options and more inside debt. Using mergers of financial institutions that increase or decrease dual ownership in portfolio firms, the paper identifies a causal link between dual ownership and CEO compensation. Mutual fund proxy-voting data suggest that shareholder voting is an important channel through which dual holders implement less convex pay contracts.

### Tariff uncertainty and firm innovation: Evidence from the U.S.–China Permanent Normal Trade Relation

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/tariff-uncertainty-firm-innovation-jef-2021/
- Authors: Tao Chen, Huasheng Gao, Yuxi Wang
- Published: Journal of Empirical Finance 62: 12–27, 2021. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jempfin.2021.02.002
- PDF: https://papers.ssrn.com/sol3/Delivery.cfm?abstractid=3396232 (Working-paper version (SSRN), titled “Effects of Chinese Imports on U.S. Firm Innovation”)
- Keywords: tariff uncertainty; innovation; patents; Permanent Normal Trade Relations; U.S.-China trade
- In one sentence: Lower uncertainty about future tariffs on Chinese imports led affected U.S. firms to innovate more.
- Summary: The paper examines how tariff uncertainty on Chinese imports affects U.S. firm innovation. It uses the U.S. grant of Permanent Normal Trade Relations (PNTR) to China, which reduced uncertainty about future tariff increases on Chinese goods. U.S. firms affected by PNTR significantly increase their patents and patent citations relative to other firms. The effect is stronger for firms with more irreversible investment and for firms that saw a larger rise in Chinese imports after PNTR. The evidence is consistent with lower tariff uncertainty making long-term, irreversible investment such as innovation more attractive.

### Marginal cost of risk-based capital and risk-taking

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/marginal-cost-risk-based-jbf-2019/
- Authors: Tao Chen, Jing Rong Goh, Shinichi Kamiya, Pingyi Lou
- Published: Journal of Banking & Finance 103: 130–145, 2019. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbankfin.2019.03.011
- PDF: https://dr.ntu.edu.sg/server/api/core/bitstreams/1fb0e88d-1050-44a5-ab23-eef7f1b846e5/content (Accepted manuscript (DR-NTU repository))
- Keywords: risk-based capital; insurers; risk-taking; capital regulation; systemic risk
- In one sentence: A diversification feature of risk-based capital rules leads insurers with lower marginal capital costs to buy riskier bonds.
- Summary: The paper shows that a built-in diversification benefit in the risk-based capital (RBC) system, which comes from how risk categories are aggregated, creates moral hazard for insurers. Insurers facing lower marginal RBC costs on fixed-income investments buy riskier fixed-income securities, even when the lower cost results from higher risk in other categories, an unintended consequence of the RBC square-root rule. Using Hurricanes Katrina and Sandy as shocks to RBC costs, insurers that suffered more took more fixed-income risk and saw their overall risk rise. Insurers with high RBC costs also sold similar risky bonds during the financial crisis, a possible source of systemic risk.

### Windfalls of emperors' sojourns: Stock market reactions to Chinese firms hosting high‐ranking government officials

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/windfalls-emperors-sojourns-stock-smj-2017/
- Authors: Douglas A. Schuler, Wei Shi, Robert E. Hoskisson, Tao Chen
- Published: Strategic Management Journal 38(8): 1668–1687, 2017. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1002/smj.2622
- PDF: https://dr.ntu.edu.sg/server/api/core/bitstreams/7b473f91-25ea-4a43-a863-f3716aa6bf51/content (Accepted manuscript (DR-NTU repository))
- Keywords: corporate political activity; government officials; event study; stock market reaction; China
- In one sentence: Investors react positively when Chinese firms host visits by the President or Premier, especially private firms and firms with weaker prior performance.
- Summary: The paper contributes to research on corporate political activity by showing that investors value firms that host visits by China’s President or Premier. Investors may value such visits because they signal future access to government-controlled resources and because high-ranking visitors certify the firm’s reputation and legitimacy. An event study of 84 such visits from 2003 to 2011 shows positive stock-market reactions for host firms relative to comparable non-host firms in the same industry. The largest reactions are for firms with weaker prior financial performance and for private rather than state-controlled firms.

### How does analysts' forecast quality relate to corporate investment efficiency?

- Page: https://taochen.org/research/analysts-forecast-quality-relate-jcf-2017/
- Authors: Tao Chen, Lingmin Xie, Yuanyuan Zhang
- Published: Journal of Corporate Finance 43: 217–240, 2017. DOI: https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jcorpfin.2016.12.010
- PDF: https://dr.ntu.edu.sg/server/api/core/bitstreams/1a5312a0-9174-4d34-b97c-1002ab374cd4/content (Accepted manuscript (DR-NTU repository))
- Keywords: financial analysts; forecast quality; investment efficiency; information asymmetry; monitoring
- In one sentence: Higher-quality analyst forecasts are associated with more efficient corporate investment, reducing both under- and over-investment.
- Summary: The paper examines how financial analysts affect the efficiency of firms’ investment decisions, using the accuracy and dispersion of analysts’ earnings forecasts as measures of forecast quality. High forecast quality is associated with more investment when a firm is likely to under-invest and less investment when it is likely to over-invest, so forecast quality increases investment efficiency. The effects are stronger for firms with higher information asymmetry and lower institutional ownership. The results are consistent with better analyst forecasts improving the information environment and external monitoring.
